name: Lac Abbé
subtitle: Lake Abbe is a salt lake on the border between Djibouti and Ethiopia, the last of a chain of six lakes fed by the Awash River.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Straddles the border between Ethiopia and Djibouti; largest and last of a chain of six lakes fed by the Awash River

facts.label: Geology
facts.value: Salty and dotted with hot springs; lies at the junction of the Arabian, Nubian and Somalian plates

facts.label: Volcanoes
facts.value: Surrounded by rift volcanoes, the largest being the shield volcano Dama Ali to the northwest

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 34,000 ha of open water and 11,000 ha of surrounding salt flats that can extend 10 km from the water's edge (Ethiopian side factsheet)

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: Records give a maximum depth of 37 m (mean 8.6 m)

facts.label: Water source
facts.value: The Awash is the only source of fresh water for Lakes Abe and Afambo

facts.label: Pressure
facts.value: Irrigated farms further up the Awash valley reduce the inflow of water to the lake

facts.label: Shrinkage
facts.value: Its surface area has fallen by 65% in sixty years (journalistic figure, undated article)

facts.label: Chimneys
facts.value: The limestone chimneys are in fact fumaroles that still emit hot vapours

facts.label: Name
facts.value: Abbé (or Abhé) means 'rotten' or 'stinking' in Afar, from sulphur emissions

facts.label: Tourism
facts.value: The first of the community-run tourist camps in Djibouti, inherited from the nomadic way of life, appeared in the 1990s

parts.text: Lake Abbe is a salt lake on the border between Djibouti and Ethiopia, the last of a chain of six lakes fed by the Awash River. It lies at a junction of three tectonic plates, with hot springs and limestone chimneys that emit steam. Irrigation upstream on the Awash reduces its inflow and the lake has shrunk.
